4:T46f,WebGraphMix operates on the Common Crawl host-level hyperlink graph. Each node is a host, and each directed edge is a hyperlink between hosts. The graph used in the paper has 13.9M nodes and 439.6M edges. The method computes centrality scores on this graph, maps each document to the score of its host, and then constructs pretraining mixtures that emphasize central hosts, peripheral hosts, or a controlled combination of both. The main centrality measures are betweenness centrality and Katz centrality. Betweenness captures bridge-like nodes that lie on many shortest paths, while Katz centrality captures influence propagated through links to other influential nodes. The authors also test PageRank, but it does not improve results, matching a similar observation in DCLM. The experiments are integrated into the DataComp-LM pipeline, with tokenization, shuffling, and optimization held fixed to isolate the effect of data selection. The paper also combines graph centrality with the DCLM-fasttext quality classifier using multiplicative and divisive scoring, testing whether topology adds information beyond content-based quality.5:T71d,The method has three layers: formalizing entity-level membership inference, designing prompt-based interrogation strategies, and turning model responses into a binary membership decision through semantic features.

The task definition is the first important step. Given a target entity and a small set of related clues, the attacker must decide whether information about that entity was used in training. The setting is label-only black-box: no logits, no gradients, no training data access, only textual outputs from queries. That makes the setup stricter and more realistic for auditing closed models.

The central intuition is related information leakage. If a model has been exposed to an entity during pretraining, then partial clues about that entity should make it more likely to reveal additional consistent information. Rather than using open-ended multi-turn dialogue, the authors distill six classic interviewing paradigms and instantiate five concrete interrogation strategies under a unified prompt template. The choice to avoid dynamic dialogue is deliberate: multi-turn interactions are harder to reproduce, harder to featurize, and more vulnerable to compounding errors.

At inference time, responses generated under each strategy are paired using two pairing schemes, converted into semantic similarity vectors, and fed into a binary classifier. So the method does not rely on exact fact matching. Instead, it uses the pattern of semantic consistency between clues and elicited responses as evidence of training exposure. This is more robust than keyword heuristics and more standardized than free-form judging. The paper also includes a theoretical analysis of feasibility under clue, input, and model constraints, aiming to characterize when entity-level inference is possible and where its limits lie.6:T4f4,The authors build dedicated datasets for entity-level membership inference and evaluate separately on person and organization entities. The main result is that all five entity-level strategies outperform strong sample-level label-only baselines. For person entities, the gains over the strongest baseline are 6.0%–17.5% in Balanced Accuracy and 0.072–0.17 in AUC. For organization entities, the proposed methods still maintain an advantage, but the task becomes harder for everyone.

That degradation on organizations is plausible and informative: organization names are often more ambiguous, their contexts are more diverse, and public evidence is noisier, which makes entity boundaries less clean. The paper also tests transfer across target LLMs with different scales and architectures. Reported differences across target models stay within 5.0% in Balanced Accuracy and 0.036 in AUC, suggesting the framework is not tightly coupled to one model family, although TPR@1%FPR remains model-dependent. If the full paper includes ablations, the most useful ones to inspect are the complementarity of the five interrogation strategies, the contribution of the pairing schemes and semantic features, and the sensitivity to clue quantity, clue quality, and entity type.7:T639,The main method is a parallel-corpus audit of tokenizers. The authors argue that non-parallel corpora confound language effects with topic, register, and sentence-length differences. By holding meaning constant across translations, differences in token counts can be attributed more directly to the interaction between language, script, morphology, and tokenizer vocabulary coverage. They evaluate 20 African languages against 11 current frontier and open tokenizers.

The metric design is careful. After Unicode NFC normalization, they compute word count, token count, character count, and UTF-8 byte count under a fixed convention shared across all languages. Token counts exclude BOS/EOS and other special tokens to avoid sequence-overhead artifacts. Word segmentation follows a uniform Unicode UAX-29 rule rather than language-specific heuristics, prioritizing comparability over linguistic tailoring. The paper then derives five metrics: fertility (tokens per word), premium relative to English, characters per token, bytes per token, and context efficiency under a fixed window size. Corpus-level aggregation uses sum-then-divide rather than mean-of-ratios, which is the right choice for stability.

A practical contribution is the translation of fertility into deployment-facing quantities: USD and local-currency costs, latency multipliers, and effective context-window erosion. This makes the tokenizer issue legible to system builders, not just NLP researchers. The inclusion of local-currency volatility in the cost model is also a realistic touch for the target deployment setting.8:T4d5,From the provided full-text content, the study evaluates 20 African languages and 11 tokenizers, with corpus-level aggregation and bootstrap confidence intervals. The language set spans multiple script families and morphological profiles, including Latin, Geʿez/Ethiopic, Arabic/Ajami, and N’Ko, which should make the analysis more informative than a generic multilingual average. The paper also instantiates the cost model in three deployment scenarios: bank customer service, clinical triage, and agricultural SMS assistance.

What is not fully visible in the provided text is the exact leaderboard of premiums, the worst-case language–tokenizer pairs, and the detailed ranking differences across tokenizers. So it would be unsafe to invent precise headline numbers. What is clear is the intended empirical claim: African languages incur a measurable and often substantial tokenization penalty relative to English, and that penalty compounds into higher cost, slower generation, and reduced effective context capacity. When reading the full paper, the most important results to inspect are the premium distributions by language and tokenizer, the script-family effects, and the relative context efficiency at the 128k window size.9:T45a,For a skim read, start with the introduction and the metrics section. Those two parts determine whether the measurement setup is credible. Focus on three design choices: why parallel corpora are necessary, why fertility is aggregated with sum-then-divide, and why bytes-per-token and context efficiency are reported alongside tokens-per-word. Then move to the main result tables or leaderboard plots to see which tokenizers are consistently better or worse for African languages and which scripts are most penalized. Finish with the cost model and deployment scenarios to judge whether the analysis maps cleanly to real production constraints.

A 25 to 35 minute read should be enough for the main thread. If reading more carefully, spend time on the appendix sections covering corpus construction, segmentation implementation, preprocessing edge cases, and bootstrap details. Measurement papers often live or die on these choices. One additional question worth checking is how sensitive the absolute fertility values are to the chosen word-segmentation standard for languages that do not align neatly with UAX-29.a:T812,All experiments hold the fraction of tokens from repeated content fixed at f=0.1, matching the setup of prior landmark work to enable direct comparison, with 90% of training tokens drawn from deduplicated FineWeb-Edu-Dedup and the remaining 10% drawn from a fixed repeated document pool. Under the fixed-f constraint, repeated pool size is inversely proportional to per-document repeat count R (higher R corresponds to a smaller repeated pool); the combination of pool size and R is termed repetition structure, the core independent variable in experiments. Models are Qwen3-style decoder-only Transformers spanning 34M to 344M parameters, trained across overtraining multipliers of 0.25x, 0.5x, 1x, 2x, and 4x the Chinchilla-optimal token budget, with R swept from 1 (no repeats) up to 20000. A no-repetition Chinchilla scaling law is fit on baseline runs to define Compute-Equivalent Gain (CEG), the ratio of no-repetition compute required to match a repeated run's validation loss to the repeated run's actual compute; Compute-Equivalent Loss (CEL = 1 - CEG) captures the fraction of compute wasted to repetition, with CEG=1 indicating parity with the no-repetition baseline. Closed-form train and test losses are derived for a misspecified linear regression setup with verbatim duplicated samples, to test whether observed damage patterns require LM-specific mechanisms. Three core findings emerge: (1) at fixed repeated token fraction, performance damage varies non-monotonically with R, with moderate repetition of a mid-sized pool causing substantially more damage than either few repeats of a large pool or many repeats of a very small pool; (2) the repeat count at peak damage R_peak follows a power law R_peak ∝ N^{-0.96} with model parameter count N, such that worst-case configurations are predictable directly from model scale; (3) the non-monotonic damage peak is fully reproduced in the linear regression toy model, confirming the pattern arises from the statistical structure of duplicated samples, not LM-specific architecture or optimizer design.b:T46e,Start with the non-monotonic damage curves in Section 4.1 to build intuition for why moderate repetition of a mid-sized pool is most harmful. The power-law fit for R_peak in Section 4.2 is the core actionable result for predicting repetition risk across scales. The CEG/CEL definition and scaling law fitting procedure in Section 4.3 is critical for understanding how raw performance gaps are converted to compute waste estimates. The toy model derivation in Section 4.4 helps avoid misattributing non-monotonic damage to LM-specific mechanisms. First, the backbone keeps DeepSeekMoE and Multi-Token Prediction, which signals continuity with an already validated large-scale recipe rather than a wholesale paradigm shift. Second, the key architectural change is a hybrid attention design combining Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA). CSA compresses KV caches along the sequence dimension and then applies DeepSeek Sparse Attention, aiming to reduce long-sequence cost while retaining selective access. HCA compresses KV more aggressively but keeps dense attention, trading more compression for a simpler attention pattern. The combination suggests that no single compression mode is sufficient across the stack. Third, the model introduces Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) in place of standard residual pathways and adopts the Muon optimizer. This is important because at 1M context and trillion-scale MoE size, optimization geometry and training stability become first-order concerns. Fourth, the training system is heavily engineered: a single fused MoE kernel overlaps compute, communication, and memory access; TileLang is used as a DSL for productivity/performance balance; deterministic, batch-invariant kernels are provided for bitwise reproducibility; tensor-level checkpointing extends autograd for fine-grained recomputation; hybrid ZeRO and two-stage contextual parallelism are used to manage compressed attention efficiently. Fifth, inference and post-training are also co-designed: heterogeneous KV-cache structures with on-disk storage enable shared-prefix reuse, and FP4 quantization-aware training is applied to MoE expert weights and the indexer QK path during post-training to reduce memory and compute.e:T4a6,The most informative numbers are straightforward. If time is limited, read Figure 1, the attention-design section, the systems section, and the main base/long-context result tables.10:T77b,The analysis first formalizes Shrinkage Bias: for non-uniform floating-point grids like E2M1, representable values follow geometric spacing, creating asymmetric rounding bins where the interval midpoint sits closer to the smaller-magnitude value. Under Round-to-Nearest-Even (RTNE, the default deterministic rounding for NVFP4), this structure produces a consistent negative expected rounding error. The bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers, rather than averaging out as zero-mean noise. The original intuition for choosing E2M1 was that non-uniform grids provide better dynamic range for heavy-tailed natural tensors; however, RHT—applied to spread outlier energy and improve codebook utilization—transforms tensor distributions to near-zero, approximately Gaussian shape, which falls exactly in the value range where E2M1 bin asymmetry is most severe, amplifying bias instead of reducing quantization error. Uniform grids (E1M2, INT4) use equal spacing between representable values, eliminating this geometric asymmetry entirely; these grids also match the post-RHT near-Gaussian tensor distribution, converting RHT-induced codebook utilization gains into consistent quantization quality. The resulting UFP4 recipe makes two core design choices: first, apply RHT to all three linear layer GEMMs in training (forward pass, data gradient, weight gradient), resolving the prior failure mode of training collapse when using RHT across all paths with E2M1; second, restrict stochastic rounding exclusively to quantization of the upstream gradient dY, using deterministic RTNE for weights and activations to minimize update variance. Unlike prior E2M1-based methods that stack stabilization fixes around a fixed format choice, UFP4 resolves the fundamental mismatch between format geometry and post-RHT tensor distribution, enabling stable end-to-end FP4 training without complex heuristic stabilization.11:T4dc,Validation spans full long-run pretraining runs at three scales: 1.5B dense, 7.9B MoE, and 124B MoE. On the 124B MoE task, well-tuned E2M1 baselines (following NVFP4 best practices) show clear loss degradation relative to BF16, with occasional late-training instability; UFP4 achieves substantially lower relative loss degradation with stable training dynamics across the entire run. Key ablation findings include: (1) Shrinkage bias accumulates with network depth for E2M1, causing measurable signal decay in deeper layers that is absent for uniform grids; (2) RHT increases bias and reduces quantization SNR for E2M1, but improves quantization SNR for uniform grids across all GEMM paths; (3) Restricting stochastic rounding to dY is sufficient—applying SR to weights or activations provides no stability benefit but increases update variance; (4) Scaling analysis across 1B to 124B parameter models shows UFP4 maintains a constant small gap to BF16, while the E2M1 gap grows with training steps and model scale; (5) Fused kernel benchmarks show UFP4 has marginally lower runtime overhead than optimized E2M1 NVFP4 implementations, as uniform quantization requires simpler per-block arithmetic, with no additional hardware support barriers.12:T4e3,OVIG is an optimistic verifier with three core components. (1) Gradient-boundary verification: the provider records weight and gradient-related evidence at intervals, and the owner locally replays a small sample of steps on potentially heterogeneous hardware. Observed gradient deviations are compared against an empirically calibrated percentile boundary derived from short calibration runs, so benign cross-device drift is tolerated while real deviations are flagged. (2) Stride-based optimistic audit protocol: the training trajectory is partitioned into intervals of size s, only interval endpoints are retained, and evidence is committed via Merkle-tree roots anchored on-chain. During audit, only sampled intervals are opened, drastically reducing storage and transmission. (3) Threat model is scoped to gradient-visible attacks (skipped steps, reduced precision, targeted gradient perturbation) rather than full semantic safety of the final model. Compared with replay-based methods like Proof-of-Learning that rely on scalar endpoint distance, OVIG inspects local gradient behavior; unlike forced deterministic replay, it accepts numerical drift; unlike cryptographic / TEE approaches, it does not require special hardware or heavy primitives.13:T641,The iterate average optimization problem is formalized as a continuous-time optimal control problem: noisy gradient descent near a quadratic minimum is approximated by the standard Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, with the control objective of minimizing squared error of the returned iterate average subject to a quadratic penalty on control magnitude, forming a solvable linear-quadratic stochastic control problem. The optimal controller applies two corrective forces to the live iterate: pulling it toward the estimated optimum, and pulling it toward consistency with the accumulated trajectory average, to prevent the live weights from drifting too far from the average. Since the exact optimal controller requires unavailable quantities during training (true optimum location, loss Hessian), practical heuristics are applied: the EMA of iterates is used as a proxy for the optimum, reducing the control term to a simple pull of live weights toward their EMA. The resulting PACE algorithm requires only one extra copy of model weights, identical to standard EMA overhead, with no additional complex state. Formal analysis establishes two key results: (1) for general convex losses with unbiased gradients, PACE achieves the standard SGD convergence rate up to a constant factor dependent on EMA strength, meaning it is never substantially worse than SGD; (2) in the quadratic setting used for derivation, PACE strictly reduces the limiting mean squared error of the averaged estimator relative to uncontrolled SGD with EMA, with arbitrarily large improvements possible on specific quadratic instances.14:T5ee,Start with the problem framing to understand the core misalignment between standard optimization targets and the deployed averaged model, the most important conceptual contribution of the work. When reading the optimal control derivation, focus on the intuition behind the control term rather than the full control theory formalism: the core idea is active shaping of the training trajectory to stay close to the average, rather than passive post-hoc computation of an average after training completes. Compare PACE to existing averaging approaches when reviewing the algorithm definition: standard EMA does not affect the training trajectory at all, Schedule-Free computes gradients at the averaged point, while PACE computes gradients at the live iterate and only adds a lightweight pull toward the EMA. When reviewing experiments, pay particular attention to constant learning rate results; robust training without learning rate decay would eliminate a major source of tuning cost in large-scale training. Granular convex convergence proofs can be skimmed for high-level results without step-by-step derivation. Note that current pretraining experiments are limited to small-scale Chinchilla-optimal setups, and validation at larger parameter scales remains open. Extensions to consider include how pull strength should be scheduled across model sizes and training phases, and whether PACE can replace existing EMA plus learning rate decay cooldown recipes in large-scale pretraining to deliver better final models.15:T427,Each dataset defines a gradient update operator U_D(θ)=θ−ηg_D(θ). For two sources A and B, the leading-order difference between U_B(U_A(θ0)) and U_A(U_B(θ0)) is governed by the commutator b_AB = H_B g_A − H_A g_B. Projecting this vector onto the target gradient gives σ_AB(E)=〈g_E, b_AB〉, whose sign predicts which order should give lower target loss. For pairwise planning, the paper evaluates the target gradient at a Trotter reference point θ_ref=θ0−η(g_A+g_B), which approximates the shared first-order drift of both orders and reduces target-gradient drift error. For many-domain scheduling, pairwise preferences define a weighted Lie-Bracket Tournament. The scalable variant deliberately uses a shared θ0 target-gradient reference. With Hessian symmetry, each source needs one Hessian-vector product u_i=H_i g_E(θ0), and Borda or row-sum scores can be computed without materializing the full O(N^2) edge matrix. This changes the estimator relative to the pairwise Trotter version, but makes the ranking procedure practical for large N.16:T4f7,GRACE parameterizes verification granularity continuously with g∈[0,1]: g=0 is outcome-only scoring (ORM), g=1 is step-level scoring (PRM), and intermediate g corresponds to verifying every few steps. The framework couples:
1) A compute model: per-sample generation cost C_gen and verification cost C_ver(g)=c0+c1·g, yielding the number of candidates N(g)=C/(C_gen+c0+c1·g).
2) A difficulty/accuracy model: δ for base success rate of sampled chains; α(g) for verifier accuracy, assumed monotone increasing and Lipschitz in g.
3) A performance objective F(g;C,δ,α): probability of selecting a correct answer among N(g) candidates using the verifier at granularity g.
The key analytical move is decomposing the marginal effect of increasing g into a non-negative “precision gain” term (better discrimination) and a non-positive “sample loss” term (fewer candidates). Under additional regularity assumptions (including log-concavity), they derive a critical compute threshold C* such that coarse verification is optimal below C* and fine verification is optimal above C*, i.e., a regime transition. Building on this, GRACE-Adapt estimates instance difficulty online and selects g adaptively to approach the Pareto-optimal frontier without knowing δ upfront.17:T42e,The model is a Transformer over jet point clouds. Each jet is represented as a set of constituent particles, with kinematic features, trajectory displacement features, and particle identification features. The architecture uses a learnable class token, pre-norm Transformer blocks, SwiGLU feed-forward layers, and no positional encodings because the input is a set. Depth is fixed at four layers and the attention head dimension is fixed at eight; embedding width and number of heads are varied to obtain 12 model sizes from roughly 3K to 10.5M parameters. Pretraining uses JetClass-II, which contains 188 simulated jet classes grouped into QCD, two-prong BSM resonance decays, and three/four-prong BSM resonance decays. Four pretraining subsets are compared: QCD only, QCD plus res2p, QCD plus res34p, and the union of all three groups. The downstream task is 10-class jet classification on JetClass. The main design choice is to use BSM resonance decays as a controlled way to increase both distributional diversity and alignment with downstream substructure features.18:T8c7,The article starts from older learning-curve literature, including Amari, Hestness, and Rosenfeld, to make the point that power-law behavior predates modern LLMs. In that framing, scaling laws are empirical descriptions of how error changes with capacity, data, and compute. It then revisits Kaplan et al.: test loss scales as a power law with parameter count N, dataset size D, and compute C, and the joint form implies that overfitting is largely controlled by a ratio like N^(alpha/beta)/D. The important caveat is that Kaplan’s compute-optimal recommendation depends on the experimental range and fitting procedure, which pushed the optimum toward larger models trained on relatively fewer tokens.

The Chinchilla section is the core. It breaks down three fitting strategies. Method 1 fixes model size and varies the token budget to identify the best token count per model. Method 2 uses IsoFLOP profiles, comparing different N–D allocations under fixed total compute. Method 3 fits a parametric joint loss function directly. The article explains why these are not interchangeable: token sweeps reveal undertraining more directly, IsoFLOP studies align better with real compute allocation, and parametric fits are efficient but sensitive to functional assumptions and sampling coverage.

A particularly useful part is the discussion of fitting pitfalls. If experiments are concentrated in a narrow region, especially one that is effectively data-infinite or strongly model-limited, the fitted exponents can be systematically biased. If partially trained runs are treated as if they reflected compute-optimal behavior, the resulting recommendation will favor oversized, undertrained models. The toy simulation makes this concrete: even when the ground-truth law is known, limited coverage and noise can produce stable but wrong exponents. That is the real reconciliation between Kaplan and Chinchilla: not a simple contradiction, but different estimation procedures operating under different regimes.

The final section on why power laws appear is interpretive rather than formal. It argues that away from tiny-scale and saturation regimes, many error terms behave approximately scale-free, which makes log-log linearity empirically robust.19:T625,This is a synthesis article rather than a new empirical paper, so the emphasis is on reinterpreting existing results and fitting procedures. It revisits Kaplan 2020: Transformer language models with roughly 768M to 1.5B non-embedding parameters, datasets from 22M to 23B tokens, trained with 3k-step warmup and cosine decay. One key Kaplan conclusion was N_opt ∝ C^0.73, implying that a 10x compute increase should scale model size by about 5.5x but tokens by only about 1.8x. The article highlights that this is exactly the recommendation later corrected by Chinchilla because it leaves models substantially undertrained.

For Chinchilla, the main takeaway is that compute-optimal scaling is much closer to growing parameters and training tokens in the same rough order, meaning smaller models trained on more data under a fixed compute budget. The excerpt provided here does not enumerate every number from the original Chinchilla study, but the experimental lesson is clear: once token sweeps or IsoFLOP comparisons are done carefully, many Kaplan-style large-model points are revealed to be undertrained, which shifts the optimum toward more tokens and fewer parameters.

The most informative “experiment” in the article is the toy simulation. It shows that the fitting pipeline itself can create bias: narrow sampling ranges, noise, and overly rigid parametric assumptions can all distort the inferred exponent and the downstream compute-optimal prescription. For anyone running internal scaling studies, that lesson matters more than any single fitted exponent.1a:T63b,This is a unified evaluation and controlled-analysis paper. The authors evaluate eight modern DLMs, covering both pure diffusion and block-diffusion families, and compare them against strong autoregressive baselines under a shared protocol. The key contribution is not a catalog of model internals, but a decomposition of the main degrees of freedom that govern DLM behavior. First, they run a unified downstream evaluation across eight benchmarks spanning general knowledge, reasoning, coding, and machine translation, instead of letting each model be judged on a different task mix. Second, they treat inference budget as a first-class variable: denoising steps, sequence length, block size, and unmasking ratio are explicitly analyzed rather than hidden as implementation details. Third, they run controlled small-scale scaling experiments under matched training conditions to compare perplexity and scaling behavior with fewer confounds from data and compute differences. Fourth, they add a systems view by reporting peak memory and FLOPs not only for a single forward pass but for full generation. The most informative comparison is between pure diffusion and block diffusion. Pure diffusion offers stronger global parallel refinement in principle, but often requires many denoising rounds. Block diffusion tries to recover some of that flexibility while reducing total generation cost through local blockwise generation and conditioning. The paper’s contribution is to place these design choices into one experimental framework and study how they affect quality, efficiency, and scaling.1b:T566,The experiments appear in three main groups. The first is the unified benchmark evaluation: eight DLMs are compared with autoregressive baselines on eight tasks covering knowledge, reasoning, coding, and translation. The authors emphasize comparable inference budgets rather than paper-specific best-case settings. The second group is hyperparameter and decoding ablations: they study how performance changes with more denoising steps, where diminishing returns begin, how sequence length and block size affect both quality and cost, and how parallel unmasking trades off throughput against output quality. The third group is computational analysis: peak memory and FLOPs are reported for both single forward passes and complete generation, making the deployment cost of pure diffusion and block diffusion directly comparable. The abstract and introduction do not expose all numeric results, but the paper is clearly organized around a few stable conclusions: DLM performance is highly sensitive to inference hyperparameters; more denoising steps usually improve quality but with non-linear returns; block-diffusion models often sit in a more practical efficiency regime, while pure diffusion better exposes the promise of global refinement but at higher end-to-end generation cost; and controlled perplexity/scaling experiments help separate modeling effects from decoding effects.1c:T4b0,Start with the introduction and setup sections to identify which eight DLMs are included, which are pure diffusion, which are block diffusion, and what autoregressive baselines are used. Then go straight to the unified benchmark tables and the quality-efficiency curves. Those are the most decision-relevant parts of the paper. After that, read the ablations on denoising steps, block size, and unmasking ratio, because many apparent disagreements in the DLM literature are really disagreements about decoding settings. If your interest is pretraining paradigms rather than deployment, focus on the controlled scaling and perplexity sections, since they speak more directly to whether the objective and architecture are intrinsically competitive. If your interest is systems practicality, prioritize the memory and FLOPs analysis. A useful deeper reading question is whether the comparisons are truly budget-matched. Another is whether perplexity tracks downstream quality for DLMs; if not, that would suggest the need for different intrinsic evaluation tools. A third is whether block diffusion gains come from a genuinely different modeling regime or from moving closer to autoregressive structure.1d:T95e,技术路线分三层。

第一层是构造 sandbox。作者把图上的随机游走序列当作离散生成任务：节点 ID 是 token，长度为 L 的 walk 是训练样本，模型只从样本学习，从不显式看到图 G 或转移核。评测时则利用图结构做两类精确指标：一是 coherence / validity，检查相邻 token 是否真有边相连；二是 transition TV distance，从生成样本估计转移核，与真实随机游走核比较分布保真度。这个设计的好处是，latent structure 对模型是隐藏的，对研究者却是可控的，因此可以系统改变图密度、瓶颈、端点约束、Markov 阶数，观察采样器行为如何变化。

第二层是理论分析。论文先证明：在 perfect conditionals 下，单坐标 sequential unmasking 是 order-invariant 且精确的，因为它等价于链式分解；但 parallel unmasking 不再有这个性质，因为它把真实 block conditional 近似成多个单点条件分布的乘积，只有在这些坐标条件独立时才精确。作者构造了简单 DAG / graph 例子，证明 lowest-entropy 两两并行揭示有时优于 random，有时反而更差，因此任何只依赖局部 uncertainty score 的策略都不可能 uniformly optimal。关键决定因素不是 token 自身熵，而是 reveal set 内部以及与已知上下文之间的条件分离结构。

第三层是提出 bisection-style sampler。直觉来自 Markov separation：对一阶随机游走，如果先揭示中间位置，它会把左右两段在条件上分开；对 k 阶 Markov walk，则需要揭示一个大小匹配阶数的 separator block。算法上就是先揭中间 separator，再对左右子区间递归并行处理。作者证明，在 perfect conditionals 下，这个 coarse-to-fine schedule 对无条件随机游走和端点条件随机游走都可以做到精确采样；对 order-k 情况，NFE 复杂度是 O(k log(L/k))，并行深度显著低于逐点采样。

论文最后把这个思路迁移到真实文本 MDM。虽然语言不满足显式 Markov 图结构，作者仍然把“先揭能分隔依赖的锚点，再递归细化”当作 schedule 设计原则，在预训练 OpenWebText masked diffusion 模型上测试。这里的意义不在于证明语言也满足同样定理，而在于说明 graph sandbox 学到的 sampler inductive bias 可以转移到自然语言生成。1e:T8f8,The paper has three technical layers.

First, it builds a verifiable sandbox. Training data are random walks on a hidden graph. Tokens are node IDs, and the model only sees sampled sequences, never the graph or transition kernel explicitly. At evaluation time, the graph provides exact structure-aware metrics: coherence or validity, meaning whether every adjacent token pair is a legal edge, and transition total variation distance, obtained by estimating the Markov kernel from generated walks and comparing it to the true one. This gives a Sudoku-like setup where latent constraints are hidden during training but exactly testable afterward.

Second, it develops theory for sampler separations. Under perfect conditionals, sequential one-coordinate unmasking is exact and order-invariant because it follows the chain rule. Parallel unmasking is different: it approximates a block conditional by a product of coordinate-wise conditionals, which is exact only when the chosen coordinates are conditionally independent given the current context. The authors construct simple graph and DAG examples showing that lowest-entropy two-at-a-time unmasking can beat random parallel unmasking on some structures and lose on others. This rules out any claim that a purely local uncertainty score is uniformly optimal. The decisive factor is dependence structure, not uncertainty alone.

Third, the paper proposes bisection-style samplers. The idea comes from Markov separation. For first-order walks, revealing a middle position can separate the left and right halves conditionally; for order-k walks, one needs a separator block of size matched to k. The sampler reveals the middle separator, then recurses on the two sides in parallel. Under perfect conditionals, the authors prove exactness for both unconditional and endpoint-conditioned walks. For order-k Markov walks, the number of function evaluations scales as O(k log(L/k)), giving logarithmic parallel depth rather than linear sequential depth.

They then transfer the scheduling idea to a pretrained masked language model on OpenWebText. The claim is not that language literally satisfies the same graph theorem, but that the graph sandbox reveals a useful design principle: reveal dependency-separating anchors first, then refine recursively.1f:T7d2,The experiments are split between graph walks and natural language generation.

In the graph sandbox, the paper compares sequential decoding, random parallel unmasking, entropy-guided parallel policies, and bisection-style samplers. The main empirical pattern is that sampler rankings flip with graph structure. On trees and strongly coupled path-like graphs, entropy-guided parallel updates often commit too early to correlated choices, hurting coherence and transition fidelity. When extra Erdős–Rényi edges are added, creating many alternative routes, low-entropy anchors can become genuinely useful. This directly supports the theoretical claim that parallel decoding quality is governed by conditional dependence rather than uncertainty alone.

For endpoint-conditioned walks and higher-order walks, bisection-style schedules are especially effective because the separator block aligns with the underlying structure. The theoretical complexity is O(k log(L/k)) NFEs for order-k walks, and empirically these samplers achieve better validity and lower transition TV distance at similar or lower inference cost. The important point is not a single headline number, but the consistency across graph families and constraint settings.

The language experiments use a pretrained masked diffusion model on OpenWebText. There, bisection-style schedules improve the non-autoregressive speed-quality tradeoff over standard parallel schedules across MAUVE, generative perplexity, entropy, and repetition. The paper’s emphasis is not absolute quality against autoregressive baselines, but reduced quality loss at a fixed or lower number of denoiser calls.

From a pretraining perspective, two experimental aspects are especially informative. Higher-order walk results show that separator size must match the effective memory order of the target process. Endpoint-conditioned walks act like globally constrained infilling tasks and make the failure mode of naive parallel factorization much easier to see.20:T512,The framework is built on three core components: First, theoretical grounding: The order selection problem is formalized as minimizing the KL divergence between the data distribution and the distribution induced by the decoding procedure. A tractable upper bound on this intractable objective is derived, expressed in terms of the frozen denoiser's pathwise log-likelihood under teacher forcing. This bound yields a dense, model-self-aware reward signal that assigns credit to every unmasking decision: an optimal order selects the next token that maximizes the expected future log-likelihood of the remaining trajectory, rather than the token with highest local certainty. Second, Self-Aware Scheduling (SAS): A lightweight order policy is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) while keeping the base denoiser frozen. At each decoding step, the policy outputs a distribution over currently masked positions to select the next token to unmask. The policy is plug-and-play, and works seamlessly for both token-level any-order decoding and blockwise semi-autoregressive decoding. Third, optional second-stage fine-tuning: The base model is fine-tuned for a small number of steps along the learned optimal trajectories using the same self-aware objective, to deliver additional gains.21:T415,Tiered Language Models use a secret key as a permutation specification over selected parameter positions. In the public configuration, the released weights are used normally. In the keyed configuration, the same weights are partially permuted, creating an alternative computation graph. This cannot be retrofitted to an already trained model, because arbitrary parameter permutation destroys learned computation. The training recipe has two stages. First, asymmetric joint pretraining trains both public and keyed configurations on public data, while shaping gradient flow so the public configuration relies less on parameters that will later be rearranged. Second, private fine-tuning updates the rearrangeable parameters through the keyed configuration on private data, with regularization to preserve public behavior. Compared with prompt passwords, authorization is moved out of the input space. Compared with adapters, the key contains no learned weights. Compared with separate deployments, the artifact remains a single open-weight model.22:T432,The paper proceeds from a controlled ablation to a general design principle.
1) Directionality test: On a ~440M Transformer, split layers into three blocks and reallocate only FFN/MLP intermediate width (d_ff) across blocks while keeping total parameters fixed. Compare uniform vs wider-early vs wider-middle vs wider-late.
2) Tapered Language Models (TLM): replace blocky reallocations with a smooth, monotonic decay of a parameter-bearing dimension across depth under a fixed total budget. The main instantiation is tapering d_ff using linear/cosine/sigmoid schedules (cosine tends to work best). The authors argue the same principle could apply to other depth-wise capacity knobs (heads, KV dim, state size, memory slots, MoE experts), but the empirical focus is FFN tapering.
For explanation, they quantify how much each layer writes “novel” content into the residual stream: deeper-layer MLP outputs become increasingly aligned with the existing residual, consistent with refinement rather than feature creation. Tapering reduces capacity where it is less utilized.23:T406,Within each GQA group, query heads are treated as experts. With N total query experts and G KV groups, each group contains M=N/G experts that attend to the same shared KV head. For each token and each group, a router scores the M experts, applies a group-wise softmax, and selects top-k experts. The selected expert outputs are concatenated as normal hard-routed head slots, not averaged. Because hard top-k gives a weak gradient path to the router, the method adds a router-supervised weighted-sum slot, computed by renormalizing the probabilities of selected experts and summing their outputs. It also adds an always-on shared attention head to stabilize training. In the 16-query-head / 8-KV-head setting with k=1, each token computes 8 routed query experts plus one shared head; the weighted-sum slot reuses selected outputs and does not add another attention computation. The final output projection receives 10 slots rather than the 16 slots of the dense baseline, so the comparison is not strictly parameter-matched in W_O.24:T417,The paper first audits top-1 collapse warnings across 816 DLM PEFT configurations: 671 LLaDA-family configurations, 100 Dream-7B boundary configurations, and 45 MDLM-OWT 130M boundary configurations. The warning fires for every configuration, while the training loop records zero actual collapses at the 200-step horizon. The authors then explain the failure through saturation analysis. Top-1 token frequency is already 0.83±0.13 at step 0, every run is above 0.5, and the median run crosses 0.95 within four optimizer steps. The warning fire-step is not significantly associated with stability. The alternative signal is parameter-side: maximum LoRA gradient norm. A gradient routing probe shows that token CE gradients are only mildly concentrated, with Gini 0.29 and the largest evaluated token-position share at 1.5%, while LoRA parameter gradients are much more concentrated, with Gini 0.46 and one matrix carrying 63.0% of the gradient mass. The saturation analysis reports step-0 top-1 frequency of 0.83±0.13, all runs above 0.5, median crossing 0.95 within four optimizer steps, and no significant relation between legacy fire-step and stability, with Mann–Whitney U p=0.20. For max-gradient, unstable configurations in LLaDA2.0-mini have a 3.23x higher median max-gradient norm than stable ones, with n=144, Bonferroni-corrected p=2.7e-7, and bootstrap 95% CI [2.76, 3.97].
